questions.question: What is S3 Static Website Hosting and what type of content can it serve?
questions.answer: S3 Static Website Hosting is an S3 feature that enables serving HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and image files directly to browsers via an HTTP endpoint. It can only serve static content — it cannot execute server-side code like PHP, Node.js, or Python. For dynamic websites, you need EC2, Lambda, or Elastic Beanstalk.

questions.question: What are the two main problems with hosting a website on a public S3 bucket, and how does CloudFront solve both?
questions.answer: Problem 1: Latency — if the bucket is in Mumbai, users in Australia or Canada experience high latency because data travels thousands of kilometres. Problem 2: Security — opening the bucket to the public internet violates many organisations' security policies. CloudFront solves both: it caches content at global edge locations (fixing latency) and OAC keeps the bucket private (fixing security).

questions.question: What is OAC (Origin Access Control) and why is it preferred over making an S3 bucket public?
questions.answer: OAC is a CloudFront feature that restricts S3 bucket access so only a specific CloudFront distribution (identified by its Distribution ID) can read from the bucket. The bucket remains completely private — its public endpoint returns 403 Forbidden. This is preferred because it removes the security risk of exposing your storage layer to the internet, while still delivering content globally through CloudFront.

questions.question: What three things must you provide when creating a CloudFront distribution?
questions.answer: (1) Origin — the source of your content, in this case the S3 bucket. (2) Default Root Object — the file to serve when users hit the root URL, typically index.html. (3) Permissions (OAC) — Origin Access Control configuration that specifies which CloudFront distribution is allowed to read from S3, keeping the bucket private.

questions.question: What is Route 53 and what role does it play in the S3 + CloudFront architecture?
questions.answer: Route 53 is AWS's authoritative DNS service. In the static website architecture, Route 53 maps a friendly custom domain name (like www.mycompany.com) to the CloudFront distribution endpoint (dxxxxx.cloudfront.net) using an ALIAS record. Without Route 53, users would need to remember the cryptic CloudFront URL.

questions.question: What is the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss in CloudFront?
questions.answer: A cache hit occurs when the requested file is already cached at the nearest CloudFront edge location — it is served immediately without contacting S3 (fast, low latency). A cache miss occurs when the file is not cached — CloudFront must fetch it from the S3 origin, cache it at the edge, then serve it. The default TTL is 24 hours, after which cached objects expire and CloudFront re-fetches from origin.

questions.question: What is Boto3 and what are the two ways to interact with AWS services using it?
questions.answer: Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python, allowing developers to interact with AWS services programmatically from Python code. The two interfaces are: (1) boto3.resource() — high-level, object-oriented API (easier to use for common operations). (2) boto3.client() — low-level API with direct access to all service parameters (more control, more verbose).

questions.question: Why are AMI IDs region-specific, and what problem does this cause for developers?
questions.answer: AMI IDs are region-specific because AWS maintains separate copies of OS images in each region for performance and availability. The same Ubuntu Server image has a completely different AMI ID in Mumbai vs Singapore vs N. Virginia. This causes problems for developers who hardcode an AMI ID — the script works in one region but fails with 'AMI not found' in another. The fix is to always look up the AMI ID for the target region and parameterise it in scripts.

questions.question: What is the difference between an ALIAS record and a CNAME record in Route 53?
questions.answer: Key differences: (1) Zone apex — ALIAS records can be created at the zone apex (example.com), CNAME records cannot. (2) Cost — ALIAS records pointing to AWS resources (CloudFront, ELB, S3) are free. CNAME queries are charged. (3) Resolution — ALIAS records resolve at the DNS level (AWS handles the lookup), CNAME records require an additional DNS lookup. AWS recommends ALIAS records when pointing domains to CloudFront distributions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Route 53 hosted zone?
questions.answer: A hosted zone is a container for DNS records for a specific domain (e.g., mycompany.com). When you create a hosted zone, Route 53 assigns 4 name servers. You configure your domain registrar to use these 4 name servers — this makes Route 53 the authoritative DNS for your domain. Inside the hosted zone, you create records (A, CNAME, MX, etc.) to control where different types of traffic go.

questions.question: Walk me through the complete setup process for hosting a static website using S3, CloudFront, and Route 53.
questions.answer: (Situation) Setting up a global static website with security and custom domain. (Task) Deploy all three services in the correct order. (Action) 1. Create S3 bucket, upload files, enable static website hosting. 2. Create CloudFront distribution: set S3 as origin, configure OAC, set index.html as default root object. 3. Apply the OAC bucket policy to S3 — bucket is now private. 4. Wait 5–20 min for CloudFront to deploy globally. 5. Create Route 53 hosted zone, update registrar's name servers, create ALIAS A record pointing domain to CloudFront. (Result) Customers use www.mycompany.com, Route 53 resolves to CloudFront, CloudFront serves from nearest edge, S3 bucket is never directly accessible.

questions.question: A user reports that your website is loading slowly from Australia, but you are based in Mumbai. How would you diagnose and fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Website hosted in Mumbai S3 bucket, slow for Australian users. (Task) Reduce latency for global users. (Action) Diagnosis: no CDN in place — all requests travel from Australia to Mumbai. Fix: deploy CloudFront distribution in front of S3. CloudFront caches content at the Sydney edge location. First Australian user fetches from S3 (cache miss, still slow), but all subsequent users get it from Sydney edge (cache hit, fast). Also configure OAC to keep S3 private. (Result) Australian users experience significantly lower latency after CDN caching warms up.

questions.question: You updated your website's CSS file and uploaded it to S3, but CloudFront is still serving the old version to users. What is happening and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Updated CSS in S3 but CloudFront serves stale version. (Task) Force CloudFront to deliver the updated file. (Action) The old CSS is cached at edge locations with a remaining TTL. Two solutions: (1) CloudFront Invalidation — go to CloudFront console → Invalidations → Create invalidation → specify /style.css (or /* for all files). This purges the cache immediately. (2) Versioned filenames — rename to style-v2.css so CloudFront treats it as a new object (no cached version). (Result) Users receive the updated CSS on next request. Note: invalidations cost $0.005 per 1,000 paths after the first 1,000 per month.

questions.question: Your team uses the same Boto3 script to deploy EC2 instances across multiple regions. The script fails in eu-west-1 with 'AMI not found'. How do you fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Boto3 script with hardcoded Mumbai AMI ID fails in Ireland. (Task) Make the script work across all regions. (Action) AMI IDs are region-specific. The fix is to either: (1) Create a dictionary mapping each region to its correct AMI ID and look up the right one based on the REGION variable. (2) Use AWS SSM Parameter Store which provides region-specific public AMI paths (e.g., /aws/service/ami-amazon-linux-latest/amzn2-ami-hvm-x86_64-gp2). (Result) Script dynamically selects the correct AMI ID for any target region.

questions.question: A developer wants to build a Python Flask web app where users upload profile photos that are stored in S3. Should they use the Console, CLI, or SDK? Explain.
questions.answer: (Situation) Web application that programmatically saves user uploads to S3. (Task) Choose the correct AWS access method. (Action) The AWS SDK (Boto3) is the only appropriate choice. Console and CLI require human interaction — they cannot be embedded in application code. Boto3 runs inside the Flask app: when a user submits a photo, the app calls s3.upload_file() or s3.put_object() to save the file to S3 automatically, without any human clicking. (Result) Photos are saved programmatically on every user upload. This is the standard pattern for application-level AWS integration.

questions.question: You want to run a Boto3 script on an EC2 instance without storing access keys on the server. How do you handle authentication?
questions.answer: (Situation) EC2 running Boto3 but you cannot store credentials on the server. (Task) Authenticate Boto3 securely without hardcoded keys. (Action) Attach an IAM Role to the EC2 instance with the required permissions. Boto3 automatically detects the instance's IAM role via the EC2 metadata service and retrieves temporary credentials. No aws configure needed — no keys on disk. This follows AWS security best practices: roles use rotating temporary credentials, no risk of key exposure. (Result) Boto3 script authenticates securely using the instance role.

questions.question: Your company wants to serve different website content to users in Germany vs users in the US due to data residency regulations. Which Route 53 routing policy would you use?
questions.answer: (Situation) Legal requirement to serve region-specific content based on user location. (Task) Select the correct Route 53 routing policy. (Action) Use Geolocation routing policy. Create two records for your domain: one pointing to the EU CloudFront distribution (for European users) and one pointing to the US CloudFront distribution (for US users). Route 53 determines the user's location from the DNS query source IP and routes accordingly. (Result) European users are always served EU-region content; US users receive US content — satisfying data residency requirements.

questions.question: Walk me through how DNS resolution works when a user types www.mycompany.com configured with Route 53 and CloudFront.
questions.answer: (Situation) User visits www.mycompany.com which uses Route 53 and CloudFront. (Task) Trace the complete DNS and content delivery path. (Action) 1. User's browser queries its local DNS resolver. 2. Resolver queries Route 53 (authoritative name server for mycompany.com). 3. Route 53 looks up the ALIAS A record for www.mycompany.com and returns the CloudFront distribution IP. 4. Browser connects to the nearest CloudFront edge location. 5. CloudFront checks its cache — if hit, serves immediately; if miss, fetches from S3, caches, and serves. (Result) User sees the website, served from the nearest edge location, with S3 never directly exposed.

questions.question: What is the difference between Route 53 Latency routing and Geolocation routing?
questions.answer: (Situation) Choosing between two location-aware Route 53 policies. (Task) Understand when to use each. (Action) Latency routing sends users to the AWS region with the lowest measured network latency for that user — it is performance-driven. A user in the Middle East might be routed to eu-west-1 if that has lower latency than ap-south-1. Geolocation routing sends users based on their physical geographic location regardless of latency — it is rule-driven. German users always go to eu-central-1 even if another region is faster. (Result) Use Latency for best performance; use Geolocation for compliance, content regulations, or language-based routing.

questions.question: A DevOps engineer needs to shut down all EC2 instances tagged 'Environment: dev' every night at 11pm to save costs. How would you implement this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Nightly shutdown of dev EC2 instances to reduce costs. (Task) Automate the shutdown without manual intervention. (Action) Write a Boto3 script that: (1) Uses ec2.describe_instances() with a filter for tag 'Environment: dev' and state 'running'. (2) Collects instance IDs. (3) Calls ec2.stop_instances(InstanceIds=[...]). Schedule this script using either a cron job on a management EC2 instance, or AWS Lambda with an EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) rule set to trigger at 11pm UTC. (Result) Dev instances automatically stop nightly — significant cost savings with zero manual effort.

questions.question: Compare S3 Static Website Hosting to using EC2 for a static website. When would you choose each and what are the trade-offs?
questions.answer: S3 Static Website Hosting: Zero compute cost (pay only for storage and requests), automatic scaling, no maintenance (no OS patches, no server management), 99.999999999% durability for files. BUT: only serves static content, no server-side processing. EC2: Full server control, can run any application code, supports databases and dynamic processing. BUT: must pay for instance even when idle, requires OS maintenance, patching, and security hardening, manual or Auto Scaling setup required. Choose S3 + CloudFront for any static website (portfolios, landing pages, documentation, SPAs with a separate API backend). Choose EC2 when you need server-side code execution, database access from the web tier, or custom software installed on the server.

questions.question: How would you design a highly available, globally distributed architecture for a company website that serves 10 million users per day across 6 continents?
questions.answer: The architecture: (1) S3 bucket as origin (private, OAC enabled) — store all static assets. (2) CloudFront distribution with edge locations on all 6 continents — handle global caching, SSL termination, compression. (3) Route 53 with Latency-based routing — if multiple CloudFront distributions are needed for compliance, route users to nearest. (4) AWS WAF attached to CloudFront — protect against DDoS and web attacks. (5) S3 bucket versioning enabled — easy rollback if bad content is deployed. (6) CloudFront Invalidations process for deployments — clear cache when content updates. (7) CloudFront access logs to S3 → Athena for analytics. This handles 10M users with no servers to manage, automatic global scaling, and sub-100ms response times for cached content.

questions.question: Explain how you would securely give a third-party vendor Boto3 access to upload files to a specific S3 bucket without giving them access to anything else in your AWS account.
questions.answer: The correct approach using the principle of least privilege: (1) Create an IAM user specifically for the vendor (do not use your own account). (2) Create an IAM policy that allows ONLY s3:PutObject on the specific bucket ARN: arn:aws:s3:::vendor-uploads-bucket/*. (3) Attach this policy to the IAM user. (4) Generate access keys for the IAM user and share them securely with the vendor. (5) The vendor uses these keys in their Boto3 scripts (aws configure or environment variables). (6) The vendor can only upload to that specific bucket — they cannot list buckets, read objects, access other services, or do anything else. Bonus: enable S3 bucket versioning and access logging to audit all uploads.

questions.question: What is the difference between CloudFront OAC and the older OAI (Origin Access Identity)? Why did AWS move to OAC?
questions.answer: OAI (Origin Access Identity) was the original method — a special CloudFront identity added to the S3 bucket policy. OAC (Origin Access Control) is the newer recommended replacement introduced in 2022. Key improvements with OAC: (1) Supports additional S3 features like SSE-KMS (server-side encryption with KMS keys) — OAI could not access KMS-encrypted S3 objects. (2) Supports all S3 regions including newer opt-in regions. (3) Supports dynamic requests (HTTP DELETE, PUT, POST to S3) for upload use cases. (4) Uses short-term credentials with automatic rotation instead of long-term OAI credentials. AWS recommends migrating from OAI to OAC for all new and existing distributions.

questions.question: Your Boto3 script successfully launches EC2 instances but sometimes fails with 'Request limit exceeded' errors during high-volume deployments. How would you fix this?
questions.answer: This is a Rate Limiting / API throttling issue. AWS EC2 API has rate limits on how many calls you can make per second. Fixes: (1) Implement exponential backoff with jitter — when a call fails with throttling, wait and retry with increasing delays (e.g., 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s + random jitter). Boto3 has built-in retry logic via botocore config. (2) Use batch operations where possible — EC2 create_instances() supports MinCount/MaxCount to launch multiple instances in a single API call instead of calling it 50 times. (3) Configure botocore retry settings: config = Config(retries={'max_attempts': 10, 'mode': 'adaptive'}). (4) For very high volume, consider using AWS CloudFormation or Terraform which handle retries and API management internally. Result: resilient scripts that handle throttling gracefully.
